newsitem.title: UK: British shares struggle under weight of rate worries.
newsitem.headline: British shares struggle under weight of rate worries.

text.p: The latest Confederation of British Industry report is likely to keep pressure on shares next week as interest rate fears continue to stalk a nervous London stock market.
The survey which showed the fastest growth in high street sales for eight years reinforced concerns raised by the Bank of England's recent warning of higher inflation and rate rises.
The fears have left shares struggling and the difficulty in the short term, say market strategists, is identifying what might shake the market out of its present torpor.
Rate worries have been a persistent feature since last week's unexpected rise in British interest rates and shares yesterday dropped back to their lowest levels for two months.
Since its October 21 high of 4,073.2, the FTSE 100 has slipped over 150 points, managing just four day's of gains over the period.
In mid-afternoon trading on Friday the FTSE 100 index was 14.8 points higher at 3,915.2.
Even a revival in corporate activity -- British Telecom's (BT) merger with MCI, and takeover interest returning to the utility sector -- has proved unable to lift the mood.
Despite this shares remain reasonable value, according to Charterhouse Tilney strategist Richard Jeffrey.
"They're reacting to being caught unaware by a policy change. The market wasn't expecting a rate rise... as a result it's had a much bigger impact than might have been anticipated."
A surge in U.S. stocks has been largely ignored in London and the British budget on November 26 is expected to leave investors increasingly reluctant to become involved.
Wall Street's heavy post-election gains are also raising fears that the U.S. market could be due a correction.
The Federal Reserve's policy making committee meets on November 13 and while economists expect U.S. rates to remain steady, the worry is that a rise is drawing closer.

"Consensus is still for no change but the worry is that we are at the bottom of the rate cycle in the U.S., it's just a question of when a rate rise comes through," said SG Strauss Turnbull strategist Andy Hartwill.
"The market's behaving rationally in front of those concerns and it's difficult to see where the good news comes from. A giveaway British budget will be hammered by the gilt market."
Even after the the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting is out of the way the focus on U.S. rates is unlikely to subside with a raft of economic data due in the coming week.
U.S. producer prices are due to be released on Wednesday, consumer prices and retail sales on Thursday and the week ends with capacity utilisation and industrial production figures.

British producer price figures are also scheduled next week with average earnings, unemployment and unit wage costs out on Wednesday, retail prices on Thursday and the CBI regional trends survey on Friday.

In the near term trading is expected to continue being selective with activity sparked by stock specific news such as earnings reports. That list next week includes Commercial Union, British Steel, Allied Domecq, BT, PowerGen and Railtrack.
But an additional worry for the market is that continuing sterling strength is increasing pressure on earnings forecasts.

"Forecasts for 1997 are to a significant degree predicated on renewed export growth to continental Europe. The message loudly and clearly from there is don't hold your breath; demand is on its back," said Hartwill.

"Since the beginning of August sterling is up eight percent trade-weighted. On the old Treasury four-to-one rule that equates to two percentage points on base rates and we've just had another 1/4 points for good measure."
